title: Video-rate Scanning Confocal Microscopy and Microendoscopy
protocol: Set up the resonant galvanometric mirror.
Arrange the relay optics to ensure telecentricity in the system.
Place lenses at distances equal to the sum of their focal lengths for magnification control.
Identify and place optical components at aperture planes: first scanning mirror, second scanning mirror, and back-aperture of the objective lens.
Ensure the beam entering the back aperture of the objective lens is stationary.
Relay the angle-scanned beam between conjugate telecentric planes using lenses.
Set up the fiber collimator in the optical mount.
Roughly steer the beam using the adjustment screws such that it travels in a straight line both horizontally and vertically.
Place an iris in front of the fiber collimator, adjusting the vertical height such that the beam passes cleanly through the iris center.
Move the iris away from the collimator along the beam path and observe if the beam still travels through the iris center.
Adjust the beam position on the iris using the two adjustment screws.
Place the mounted dichroic mirror in the beam path with the laser beam positioned at approximately the center of the mirror.
Rotate the mirror holder to reflect the beam at approximately 90 degrees and roughly adjust the reflection so that the reflected laser beam’s vertical height does not change.
Position a mounted resonant galvanometric mirror into the laser beam path, ensuring the laser beam is centered horizontally on the mirror surface.
Reflect the laser beam off the resonant galvo mirror at a 90-degree angle by rotating the mirror mount.
Roughly adjust the reflection off the resonant galvo mirror to maintain the same laser beam vertical height.
Set the vertical height of two irises using the laser beam reflected off the resonant galvo mirror as a reference.
Clamp the two irises down in a straight line using the screw holes on the optical breadboard as a guide.
Adjust the dichroic mirror to center the laser beam on the first iris.
Use the resonant galvo mirror to center the laser beam on the second iris.
Iteratively adjust both mirrors until the beam is aligned through both irises.
Ensure that the reflected laser beam from the resonant galvo mirror remains near its center point.
Adjust the fiber collimator mount if necessary and repeat the iterative alignment steps.
Place the first relay lens in the beam path.
Look at the spot of the laser beam on the next iris after the lens.
Vertically adjust the lens height to center the vertical center of the beam on the iris.
Horizontally adjust the lens position to fully center the beam on the iris.
Carry out the same procedure for the second lens.
Hook up the resonant galvo to its scanning unit and turn it on.
Use a white business card to track the scanning beam through the two lenses.
Mark the position of the telecentric plane at 4f from the resonant galvo where the laser beam appears stationary.
Position the standard scanning galvo mirror at the marked telecentric plane location.
Adjust the mirror height and position so that the beam at the telecentric plane strikes the exact center of the scanning mirror.
Power up the mirror control hardware and apply 0 volts to the scanning mirror input.
Carefully adjust the mirror angle to direct the beam vertically.
Gently tighten the mirror in position.
Attach the second breadboard at a 90 degree angle using 90 degree mounting brackets.
Turn off the laser and scanning electronics.
Disconnect the fiber during attachment.
Disconnect the scanning mirrors during attachment.
Bolt the mounting brackets in place securely.
Rotate the entire microscope so that the new breadboard lies flat.
Use a clamp to fix the breadboard to the working surface.
Place the first large, 2” (50 mm) diameter mirror close to the edge of the breadboard.
Rotate the mirror mount to reflect the laser beam approximately 90 degrees.
Roughly adjust the reflection off the mirror to maintain the same vertical beam height.
Place the other 2” mirror at the opposite edge of the breadboard at an orientation that directs the beam downward at a 90-degree angle.
Use the adjustment screws to ensure the beam’s vertical height does not change.
Set up two irises as in step 1.4.
Adjust the two mirrors as directed in step 1.5 to center the beam on the irises.
Place the scan lens in the beam path.
Adjust the horizontal position of the scan lens to center the laser spot on the first iris.
Adjust the vertical position of the scan lens to center the laser spot on the first iris.
At a distance of 75 mm + 300 mm from the lens, place the large 2” tube lens in the beam path.
Adjust the horizontal position of the tube lens to center the beam on the first iris.
Adjust the vertical position of the tube lens to center the beam on the first iris.
Begin scanning the resonant galvo mirror.
Begin scanning the standard scanning mirror.
Locate the laser beam at a position 300 mm after the tube lens using a business card.
Unclamp and translate the tube lens along the optical path to ensure both horizontal and vertical stationary planes overlap as closely as possible.
Re-center the vertical and horizontal position of the tube lens.
Clamp the tube lens securely in position.
Place the objective lens in the beam path.
Position the objective lens back aperture as close to the stationary plane as possible.
Set up the sample stage.
Ensure that the translation mount for z-axis motion can move over its full range without contacting the objective lens mount.
Disconnect all power supplies and fiber optics.
Rotate the microscope assembly so it rests on the breadboard holding the resonant scanning mirror.
Clamp the breadboard securely in place.
Re-connect the fiber to the collimator.
Re-connect both galvos and their control cables.
Place 0 volts on the control voltage driving the standard scanning galvo.
Place a business card or a small volume of bright dye between two coverslips on the sample stage.
Turn on the laser source.
Bring the sample into focus using the translation stage.
Maximize the laser power to make fluorescence emission from the sample visible behind the dichroic mirror.
Trace the fluorescence emission through the objective lens and back through the scanning system to the dichroic mirror.
Place a mirror behind the dichroic mirror to reflect the emission at a 90-degree angle.
Use an iris along with the mirror to direct the fluorescence beam straight and parallel to the breadboard.
Set up the confocal pinhole unit as described.
Select a spatial filter cage mount assembly from ThorLabs for optimal performance.
Mount the spatial filter unit along the fluorescence beam path and center it on the emission beam.
Install a short focal length lens or microscope objective in the unit.
Adjust the z-translation mount to focus clearly onto the pinhole surface.
Ensure the entire unit is oriented precisely along the straight line of the fluorescence beam.
Clamp the unit securely to the breadboard.
Use lens tubes and shielding to enclose the emission beam path for protection against stray light contamination.
Systematically move the confocal pinhole using adjustment knobs on the translation stage.
Perform a 2D search over the pinhole mount surface by iterative adjustment of two axes to find the position that maximizes the fluorescence signal through the pinhole.
Place the collimating lens on the cage mount after locating the maximizing position for the fluorescence signal.
Slide the collimating lens along posts until the emitted fluorescence signal is as collimated as possible using a business card.
Set up the photomultiplier tube (PMT) assembly by placing a 50 mm focal length lens in the fluorescence emission beam path.
Find the focal point of the lens using a business card and mark this position on the breadboard.
Turn off the laser completely to prevent potential damage to the PMT from stray or unattenuated light.
Position the PMT so that its active area is as close to the marked focal point as possible.
Connect the PMT assembly to the focusing lens using adjustable lens tubes.
Carefully wrap dark tape around all exposed beam paths following the pinhole.
Turn on the laser at extremely low power.
Turn on the PMT and read its voltage on an oscilloscope as the control voltage is increased.
Increase the PMT control voltage until a spike-like readout or DC offset appears on the oscilloscope screen.
Confirm that the signal arises from fluorescence by turning off the laser to observe a loss of signal.
Iteratively align the pinhole for maximum signal on the oscilloscope.
Manipulate the focusing lens z-position.
Adjust the yz translation stage.
Hook up the mirrors to the video-rate microscope hardware.
Connect the custom control boards to the microscope.
Attach the computer as diagrammed in Fig 3.
Visualize a known size standard using the imaging system.
Find the optimal resolution of the microscope.
Calculate the pixel-to-resolution constant for the imaging system.
Carefully remove the sample stage.
Replace the removed sample stage with a fiber holding stage.
Dip one end of the fiber bundle in a weak solution of dye so that fluorescence emission is generated evenly across all of the fiber cores.
Turn on the scanning system.
Adjust the fiber holder to bring the proximal end of the fiber bundle into focus.
Use translation adjustment screws to center the fiber in the scanned field.
Look at the fluorescence emission image from the proximal fiber tip while scanning.
Adjust the angle adjustment knobs to make all fiber cores evenly bright.
Re-adjust the translation position to re-center the fiber in the scanned field as needed.
Iterate through adjustments until the entire fiber tip is correctly in focus.
Gently clean the distal tip of the microendoscope using lens cleaning paper slightly wetted with HPLC-grade methanol.
Use a known size standard to measure and calculate the resolution of the microendoscope imaging system.
